:::{#exm-bernoulli-exponential-family}
#### The Bernoulli distribution is an exponential family

<!-- no-figure: the example checks an algebraic identity at two values of x -->

Let $\Rvar \sim \Bernoulli(\prob)$,
the [Bernoulli distribution](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-bernoulli) with success [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $\prob \in (0, 1)$.
Its [probability mass function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pmf) is $\prob^{\rvar} \paren{1 - \prob}^{1 - \rvar}$ for $\rvar \in \set{0, 1}$.
We rewrite it in the form of @eq-exponential-family
by collecting the factors that have the [exponent](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-basics.html#def-power-exponent) $\rvar$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pdf\paren{\rvar ; \prob}
&= \prob^{\rvar} \paren{1 - \prob}^{1 - \rvar}
&& \text{(Bernoulli mass function)}\\
&= \prob^{\rvar} \paren{1 - \prob}^{-\rvar} \paren{1 - \prob}
&& \text{(a power with a sum of exponents is the product of the powers)}\\
&= \paren{\frac{\prob}{1 - \prob}}^{\rvar} \paren{1 - \prob}
&& \text{(powers with the same exponent combine)}\\
&= \expf{\logf{\paren{\frac{\prob}{1 - \prob}}^{\rvar}}} \paren{1 - \prob}
&& \text{(a positive number is the exponential of its logarithm)}\\
&= \expf{\rvar \, \logf{\frac{\prob}{1 - \prob}}} \paren{1 - \prob}
&& \text{(the logarithm of a power is the exponent times the logarithm)}\\
&= \expf{\rvar \, \logf{\frac{\prob}{1 - \prob}}} \expf{\logf{1 - \prob}}
&& \text{(a positive number is the exponential of its logarithm)}\\
&= \expf{\rvar \, \logf{\frac{\prob}{1 - \prob}} + \logf{1 - \prob}}
&& \text{(the product of exponentials is the exponential of the sum)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The [statistic](sufficiency.qmd#def-statistic) is $\statf{\rvar} = \rvar$, and $\basemeasuref{\rvar} = 1$.
The [natural parameter](#def-natural-parameter) is the [log odds](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-log-odds),
$\natparam = \logf{\prob / \paren{1 - \prob}}$.
Inverting it gives $\prob = \expf{\natparam} / \paren{1 + \expf{\natparam}}$,
so $1 - \prob = 1 / \paren{1 + \expf{\natparam}}$,
and the last term in the exponent is $\logf{1 - \prob} = -\logf{1 + \expf{\natparam}}$.
Hence the Bernoulli distributions are an [exponential family](#def-exponential-family) with
$\logpartitionf{\natparam} = \logf{1 + \expf{\natparam}}$.

To check the algebra on data,
we use the `birthwt` data,
which record the birth weight of babies born at Baystate Medical Center in Springfield, Massachusetts [@hosmer1989applied], <!-- check-term-links: allow: "weight" here is body weight, not the weight of a matrix or model -->
as distributed in R's `MASS` package [@venables2002modern].
The variable `low` is 1 for a baby with low birth weight and 0 otherwise.
We set the success probability to the [sample mean](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-sample-mean) of `low`,
and evaluate both sides of @eq-exponential-family at the two possible values of $\rvar$.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### R

```{r}
#| label: bernoulli-exponential-family-r
#| code-fold: false
birthwt <- read.csv("data/birthwt.csv")
prob <- mean(birthwt$low)

natural_parameter <- log(prob / (1 - prob))
log_partition <- function(eta) log(1 + exp(eta))

x <- c(0, 1)
exponent <- natural_parameter * x - log_partition(natural_parameter)
exponential_form <- exp(exponent)
bernoulli <- dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob)

data.frame(x, bernoulli, exponential_form)
max(abs(bernoulli - exponential_form))
```

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: bernoulli-exponential-family-py
#| code-fold: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import bernoulli

birthwt = pd.read_csv("data/birthwt.csv")
prob = birthwt["low"].mean()

natural_parameter = np.log(prob / (1 - prob))
log_partition = np.log(1 + np.exp(natural_parameter))

x = np.array([0, 1])
exponential_form = np.exp(natural_parameter * x - log_partition)

table = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "x": x,
        "bernoulli": bernoulli.pmf(x, prob),
        "exponential_form": exponential_form,
    }
)
print(table)
print(np.max(np.abs(bernoulli.pmf(x, prob) - exponential_form)))
```

:::

The value of `prob` is `r round(prob, 3)`,
so the natural parameter is $\natparam = `r round(natural_parameter, 3)`$.
The two columns agree to within rounding error:
the largest difference is `r format(max(abs(bernoulli - exponential_form)), digits = 2)`.
:::
